subtopic: EXPRESSION OF TRIBUTES ON OCCASION OF RETIREMENT

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, the following announcement from London reached Canada just about an hour ago:
The Right Honourable Sir Winston Churchill had an audience of the Queen this evening and tendered his resignation as Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury, which Her Majesty was graciously pleased to accept.
I know that the thoughts of all hon. members, as indeed those of our fellow Canadians, are turned at this moment toward that very great statesman of our time. His decision to seek Her Majesty's acceptance of his resignation will be received with mixed feelings. All of us know that no one more richly deserves a respite from the overpowering public responsibility that high office imposes. But we shall miss a leadership which for so many years-and especially in the anxious days of war-has inspired and encouraged the people of the commonwealth of nations and indeed the whole free world.
Sir Winston, during his 80 years of restless activity, has played many parts. Few figures in history have compressed so many careers in a single life span. He has been soldier, author, painter, lecturer, journalist and statesman, and he has won recognition in all. But on this occasion peace-loving people throughout the world remember first with deepest gratitude his unequalled contribution to the cause of human freedom and peace. They recall especially that time of great adversity, when the commonwealth stood alone against the forces of nazism, and democracy was in such grave peril-how his actions and his words inspired in us then courage and hope-those qualities which were so desperately needed.
Referring to that struggle, on his 80th birthday, he said:
I have never accepted what many people have kindly said, namely, that I inspired the nation. Their will was resolute and remorseless, and it proved unconquerable ... It was the nation and the race dwelling all round the globe that had the lion's heart; I had the luck to be called upon to give the 'roar'.
We all realize that Sir Winston's contribution was infinitely beyond what his modesty would allow him to admit, and we all agree that his "roar" was one of the greatest and most memorable sounds ever to come from a human throat.
With victory won, Sir Winston could have retired secure in the knowledge that he had accomplished more in his lifetime, on behalf of his fellow men, than most men are called to do. But the restless Elizabethan spirit which possessed him, and his deep sense of public service, would not permit him even the briefest respite. He continued to devote his great talents and energies, both in opposition and in government, to the problems confronting his nation and to the cause of peace which had been so dearly won.
Canadians have been privileged to greet this great world leader many times. But I do not suppose any visit gave us greater joy than the one he made here last summer; for we were able to see for ourselves how completely he had recovered from his grave illness of two years ago. The citizens of Ottawa who lined the streets of this city during that visit will recall with warm delight how, in order to better exchange greetings with them, he climbed up on the back seat of the convertible automobile and gave them his famous victory sign.
Two months ago I had the privilege of attending the last prime ministers' conference with Sir Winston as chairman. He was immensely proud of our great commonwealth of nations, and I do not think any occasion pleased him more than to have the commonwealth leaders assembled in London to discuss the many problems confronting our association and the world at large. I know each of us there was filled with admiration and respect for the manner in which he conducted our discussions and for the brilliant analysis he gave us of the problems before us.
As Sir Winston Churchill steps down from the post of prime minister of Great Britain, I am sure that all Canadians will extend to him their most affectionate and grateful greetings and offer their sincere prayer that he and Lady Churchill may enjoy many more years of health and happiness together.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: EXPRESSION OF TRIBUTES ON OCCASION OF RETIREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that most of us here today have an uneasy feeling that the end of a great period of parliamentary

Sir Winston Churchill history has now appeared before our eyes. However, it would be wrong to suggest that the resignation of Sir Winston Churchill changes substantially the great institutions with which he has been associated for more than half a century. Of course the first impression is one of immense loss in the departure from the active parliamentary scene of the greatest parliamentarian of all time.
For fifteen years he has been the authentic leader of the free world. For fifteen years it has been his voice that has given expression to the hopes and aspirations and fortitude of people who have seen much that they cherished disappear, but have found comfort in his unwavering faith in the religious background of our life and in the strength of democracy itself to survive every change that may come.
It is a long time since the desperate days of 1940 when Britain stood alone-not alone, in fact, because there was the whole commonwealth ranged at her side, but alone in the immediate presence of the enemy. At that time words were spoken which must to many have seemed almost empty expressions of a faith that could hardly be supported by the dreadful arithmetic of war.
We will always remember how with that buoyant humour, never diminishing even in the most ominous hours, he came here to make a speech which will remain on the pages of the history of all countries which love freedom. He reminded his hearers that he had been told that if Britain fought on, separated from the nazi hordes by only a little more than 20 miles, her neck would be wrung like the neck of a chicken. There is no one here who will forget the way in which he gave his answer, the pause in his remarks when he said, "Some chicken, some neck."
It was his ability then, and in the troubled years which followed, to convey his meaning in the simple colloquial terms of the people who bear the brunt of every struggle, terms which appealed to people everywhere, because the words he used were understood in every language whatever it might be.
One of the great things about his life has been his close association at all times with the United States. Along with the great speeches that were made here in Ottawa to the people of Canada are those memorable speeches which he made in Washington. He appealed to the spirit and confidence of people with the same historic background in a way that no other man could have done. He said that if conditions had been reversed, if instead of his mother being the American member of the family it had been his father, he might have got into congress on his own.


That brought him very close to the hearts of the people of the United States. I feel sure that at this hour throughout the whole United States there is the same feeling of affection, the same feeling of respect and admiration which we cherish here, because the respect for Sir Winston Churchill and all he represents is something that is limited by no international boundary but is a common heritage of free people everywhere for all time.
His boldness in the face of immense difficulties, his challenge to the enemy who thought they were certain to prevail, rallied his own people and gave them courage and strength. It is true, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has pointed out, that he sought to play down his own part. He sought to give the impression that he had merely been the interpreter of the sentiment of the people of Britain and of the commonwealth at that time. Thank God we had such an interpreter at that hour. There might have been others who with less certain voice would not have aroused the same response.
The simple fact is that no other man in history has occupied so many roles with such distinction as has Sir Winston Churchill. He is the greatest statesman of all time and I am confident that history will declare that fact. I remember that in his own book on his early life, written long before there seemed any possibility that he might occupy such a role, he spoke of the fact that seldom had a great leader in war been a great leader in peace. He then went on to make a statement the accuracy of which some of my medical friends challenge. He said that the brain is divided into two parts, of which one controls military affairs and the other deals with problems of peace, and for that reason very rarely has one man been able to be successful in both fields. Then long before he occupied a position of any substantial importance he said, "Who knows but that I may prove the exception to the rule?"
Whether his description of the brain was accurate or not, and there are those here who are more competent to express an opinion on that than I am, the fact remains that he emerged from the years of great war leadership; he tasted defeat without bitterness; he returned to power without boasting, and he has proved himself almost as great a leader in peace as in war. In fact I hesitate to place any reservation on his peacetime achievements because I have the impression that when the history of these times is written it may well be told that almost as great as his contribution to the freedom of the world in 1940 was his contribution to the unity of the western world at the time when disharmony seemed to prevail after the collapse

of EDC last summer. I think it will be found that his immense prestige brought together nations which seemed then to be drawing apart, and that the growing unity of western Europe is a tribute to the manner in which he was able to speak to the leaders of other nations and bring them together at that time.
Fortunately we are not here to mourn him; on the contrary he is very much alive. The news reports we have received today state that he enjoyed a pleasant evening last night surrounded by his immediate friends and honoured by the presence of the Queen to whom he has rendered such magnificent service. How fitting it was that on his last day in office he should be host, with Lady Churchill, to the Queen whom he served so well; this remarkable man who had the unique opportunity to serve Queen Victoria, her son King Edward VII, King George V, King George VI and now the new and young Queen Elizabeth II. What an unparalleled service that has been to the institution of monarchy in which he so strongly believes. He is still very much alive and I prefer to believe that instead of this being, by any manner of means, the end of his activities we shall probably see this as the beginning of a new period of adventure which will greatly help all of us.
He now goes out, free from any suggestion of partisan political association, as the elder statesman not only of Britain but of all free nations. He enters that new period of adventure with a spirit of youth which he has expressed so well even during recent weeks. When I learned just a short time ago that his resignation was official-and most of us thought it would not be official for at least a few hours yet-I was reminded of these lines of Oliver Wendell Holmes, which it seems to me apply to him so aptly at this time:
Call him not old. whose visionary brain
Holds o'er the past its undivided reign.
For him in vain the envious seasons roll
Who bears eternal Summer in his soul.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of those associated with me I wish to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in the moving tributes they have paid on the occasion of the resignation of the Right Hon. Sir Winston Churchill.
On occasions like this, one is tempted to look down the long avenue of time at the history of the institution of parliament which we share in common with the people of Britain and other parts of the commonwealth, and perhaps to appraise those who are in power and exercising influence within that institution. When I heard that Sir Winston
Sir Winston Churchill
Churchill had resigned I looked back and could think of no prime minister in British history who occupies a higher place in the affections of the British people, the Canadian people and indeed of the world than Sir Winston Churchill. The only name I can think "bf that can be placed beside that of Sir*; Winston Churchill is that of William Pitl the Elder, the great Earl of Chatham. He laid in large part the foundation of this commonwealth or of the British Empire, as it was called then, and Churchill in his time has been one of the architects of the modern commonwealth.
'What a long span of history that is. No man, I think, has better expressed the ideals and the determinations of the democratic peoples of the world than has Churchill. I, of course, can look back to a time when Churchill was prominent in public life in the early part of this century as a pungent spokesman for the Liberal party. I remember him as an outstanding leader of the British commonwealth during the first war in the coalition government. I of course remember him later on sitting as an independent member in the British House of Commons, and now we realize that he has won the admiration and support of many people who have disagreed with him on occasion throughout the years.
When it came to the formation of that wartime government in 1940, despite the fact that many people had bitterly opposed many of his views, the Labour party said, "We will serve under Churchill, and under none other will we serve." And so today, as the curtain of public life is rung down as far as the prime ministership of Britain is concerned, one can only say that whether or not one agrees with the political philosophy which governs the party views of Sir Winston Churchill, I believe it is the glory of democracy, of this commonwealth and of this institution that on occasions like this we can all admire and pay tribute to the great services rendered by a statesman to the people of his day and his generation, whether or not one agrees with all his views.

Mr. Speaker, it is not often that this parliament pauses to pay tribute to a man or a woman who is still living. This therefore marks a very interesting precedent in my experience in this house. I am very glad to join with those who have spoken this afternoon to pay tribute to a man who has earned the place he now holds in the affections of everyone. I suppose it is because Sir Winston Churchill is such an amazing man that we are doing what we are doing today, breaking new ground. This man has aroused the imagina-

Inquiries of the Ministry tion and the admiration of free people in all parts of the world. Churchill surely represents the very best in British statesmanship, and for that reason he is looked to for advice, counsel and guidance, and this has been true for many years.
It is to be regretted that Churchill was not able to realize his dream of peace throughout the world while he was still in office. I imagine he would like to have stayed in office until he did realize his dream, 'but perhaps in his new-found retirement he might still be able to contribute something to the achievement of peace.
Sir Winston Churchill has earned the gratitude of many millions of people in all lands for his great services to humanity in many fields. I sincerely hope that he will have as many years as he might desire in which to enjoy his retirement, free from the responsibilities of office. And if he wishes to continue to represent his old constituency in the House of Commons I hope he will have that privilege, too.

Possibly I might say a word on that point, because I do not think the government of the United States is at fault. When the note on this matter, which was

tabled in the house, was received by the United States government we were informed that they would wish to make a reply to it in due course. We have been pressing them very hard to get it and have indicated that we would like to have it before parliament rises. subtopic: CONCERNING RESTRICTIONS ON IMPORTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would point out that this is the first occasion we have been informed it was only an oral reply. I wish to make it quite clear that there should be no discourtesy on the part of our government with regard to a matter of this kind or of any other kind in its dealings with the government of the United States. I was under the impression that there had been the ordinary formal reply and that it was merely a case of release. That was the way it appeared from what was said in the house. The extent to which I have pressed this point was related to my understanding that the formal reply had been received and that it was merely a case of securing permission to have it released. I repeat, however, that, subject to the courtesies which I hope will always be extended in the widest measure possible in dealings with the government of the United States, the people of this country will be interested in knowing what is being done with regard to a matter that has implications going far beyond the subject matter in this case which happens to be the movement of oil across our boundaries.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the
house rose at ten o'clock last evening I was saying that I, and I think all members of the house, welcomed the recommendations of the minister as outlined by him and that I felt sure organized labour throughout Canada would also welcome them although perhaps it would be somewhat regretful that he had not gone a little further. I also pointed out that I had followed very closely the entire speech of the Minister of Labour and that I appreciated very much what I term his outline of policy before he went into the details of the bill amending and consolidating the act which he proposes to bring before the house after this motion is carried. As far as certain aspects are concerned, I found it somewhat puzzling to try to tie together his policy statement and the motivation outlined by the minister with some of the details he gave following his outline of policy.
In order to make my position clear I should like to refer to what I term the policy outline as given by the minister and quote three paragraphs found on page 2663 of yesterday's Hansard. The minister said:
It will be apparent from what I have said, Mr. Chairman, that what the government is here proposing is not merely a series of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is something much more fundamental than that. We are undertaking, in fact, the most far-reaching revision of our unemployment insurance program that have been attempted in the decade and a half of its existence during the course of the seven times the legislation has been reviewed by the house.
Again, he said:
Born out of the suffering and the hardship of the great depression, the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1940 established a new dimension of social statesmanship to which all our subsequent social legislation-family allowances, the new veterans charter, old age security, the national health program, rehabilitation of civilian disabled, have faithfully conformed. It was the passage of the Unemployment Insurance Act which enabled my predecessor, who introduced it, and all his fellow countrymen, for the first time to speak of "a Canadian social security program".
One more quotation:
What we are doing today, in the new legislation which I have the honour to introduce, is adding a worthy addition to the steadily growing structure of social security that we have been building in Canada.
I am certain that no one in the house or, as a matter of fact, in Canada, will question the principle and the motivation as outlined in those words of the Minister of Labour. My puzzlement arises from the fact that in his outlining of the details he did not, in my humble estimation, carry through in the way we had a right to expect in view of the magnificent principles and objectives outlined by him in his policy statement. If this
5, 1955
Unemployment Insurance Act proposal of the minister is to be a great advance in the over-all security program of the people of Canada, I think it automatically and axiomatically follows that it should mean not only an increase in benefits to a certain group but should also definitely mean no retreat from any security measures already in effect under the legislation. In addition, it should also mean an extension so as to give greater coverage than that which has been in effect under the act up to the present time. Therefore I look forward, may I say, to a clarification of some of the details as outlined by the minister in the light of his very excellent policy pronouncements.
In his outline the Minister of Labour told us that up until now 95 per cent of all the claimants have drawn less than 30 weeks benefits. I take it, sir, it is because of that, and one or two other factors, that a change is being made to reduce the maximum payments from 51 weeks down to 30 weeks. It may not seem of major importance, but in principle I think it is. The details given to us on this matter by the minister actually mean that according to the experience of the unemployment insurance commission over the many years, 5 per cent are going to lose a security coverage which they previously had. I believe that is an important matter. The minister made a statement on this question, and I quote from page 2261 of Hansard for April 4, 1955:
Many of these one-twentieth are married woman and elderly people for whom alternative social security programs would seem to be more appropriate.
If this is an extension of Canada's security program, I am puzzled that we should have it suggested by the minister that 5 per cent are going to lose security.

Under this labour legislation, if the workers get into a dispute with their employers, they have to go through a period of collective bargaining. If that fails, then there is mediation, conciliation and arbitration. If those fail, then a strike vote is taken. On many occasions we also see workers in supply industries become unemployed. But here the government is setting up a court of its own, it chooses the personnel which is not known to the unemployed who may be claiming unemployment benefits. He has no voice in the selection of the personnel. He brings a claim before the board of referees and may obtain a favourable decision.
I wonder why the department should then appeal the decision of its own board to an umpire who may be two or three thousand miles away from the unemployed person. That person is faced with considerable delay and is sometimes put to additional expense in having the matter determined finally. Having appointed its own board of referees, having made its own selection of qualified men to make up that board, I submit that at least generally the government should accept its decision and not carry the appeal further. Certainly it should not carry the appeal further without advising the unemployed claimant of his rights and not merely suggesting to him that the matter is settled and he need not be worried about it because nothing is going to happen. Very often something does happen and the unemployed person does not know what it is all about until he gets a notification to the contrary.
My principal reason for rising is to refer briefly to a matter which was mentioned by the hon. member for Hamilton West and by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich earlier in the session, that is, the position of fishermen with respect to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I am the first to admit that there are difficulties in the way of including this industry within the act but I do not think they are insuperable. The men employed in this industry deserve every possible consideration. I know of no group who work harder, who risk their lives and health in the earning of a livelihood to the extent the fishermen do and who generally speaking are paid less for the work and sacrifice which is necessary in this type of employment.

Surely some system can be evolved whereby these men can benefit from at least a modified form of unemployment insurance. The department itself has made a study of this matter. I have here the report of a commission which made a survey of the fishing industry in 1951. This is a pretty analytical survey; it is informative and statistical and gives a fair summary of the problems confronting this industry. In the second paragraph of their conclusions, being paragraph No. 273, they state that the administrative difficulties, although appreciable, can be overcome.
I am suggesting that if the commission appointed by the department to consider this matter found, as they did quite frankly, that the administrative difficulties can be overcome, then the minister should submit to parliament machinery which would include this group of men within the framework of the act and overcome the difficulties which his officials have admitted can be overcome.
It is easy enough to say that this cannot be done, to paint a picture of the fisherman who is part labourer, partly self-employed or a share fisherman, a man who owns part of the boat, and then ask how it can be done. The simple answer is that it is done in Great Britain.

Mr. Chairman, as I
listened to the minister yesterday I concluded that this was exceptional legislation visualized by this resolution. I thought that the legislation would be in line with the advance publicity which was given the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act by the government. The more I study the legislation that is likely to be introduced in the light of the remarks made by the minister and by others, I begin to wonder just what is the primary purpose of the amendments that are to be introduced. I had thought that the primary purpose of these amendments was to make this act a more efficient measure for those who are unemployed. I am now beginning to wonder whether or not the main purpose of these amendments is to maintain the present level of the insurance fund at or around somewhere between $800 million and $900 million.
As I study the proposed amendments I am forced to conclude that certainly one important function of those amendments is to maintain the actuarial stability of the fund and I am inclined to think that more emphasis is being placed on the stabilization of this fund at the figure I mentioned than on meeting the actual needs of the people who are to be served by the unemployment insurance fund. It is true that those who experience short periods of unemployment will benefit by reason of the fact that their weekly payments will be increased both in the case of those with family responsibilities and those without. But to offset that, the maximum period of time for which these payments are to be made will be considerably decreased. Those who experience long extended periods of unemployment, as a great many do at the present time, are likely to suffer, especially if the time in which their regular unemployment insurance expires coincides with the 15th of April. A number of people have already interviewed me in this regard. Some of them interviewed me over the past week end. They were men whose regular unemployment insurance will expire on or about April 15. After that date these men will not be eligible for either regular or supplementary benefits. Therefore in some respects the legislation visualized by this resolution is disappointing, particularly in the light of present circumstances. It would offer no relief to those who are unemployed but are not now covered by unemployment insurance


and there is a considerable sector of the working force not covered at all by unemployment insurance but who are unemployed at the present time and unable to receive any benefits.
It was to be hoped that, in view of the advance publicity given to this measure by the government and in view of the present unemployment situation, the area of those eligible for benefits would be extended and some categories not now covered by unemployment insurance would be brought under that umbrella. The amendments will be of little benefit-as a matter of fact, they will be of no benefit-to those who have exhausted their unemployment benefits. They will be of no benefit to those who have not had an opportunity to fulfil the requirements of the act. They will be of no assistance to the great many young people who are unemployed simply because they cannot find jobs and who have never had an opportunity of building up a fund on which they can draw. The amendments will not benefit those who now find their family responsibilities exceedingly high in relation to the unemployment benefits, those who are now finding it extremely difficult to provide shelter and food for their families with the present unemployment insurance benefits.
Then there are a few other ways in which the measure will be disappointing. The five-day waiting period against which labour has been protesting for some considerable time apparently is to be retained. There is no mention that the five-day waiting period is to be abolished. Regulation 5A under section 35 which the hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to as a bear trap is apparently to be retained. There has been no indication that there will be any change in that regulation. I did not hear from the minister anything to indicate that the employees of unemployment insurance offices are to receive any new consideration in the matter of wages or especially in the matter of accommodation.
I have been in many of the unemployment insurance offices in and around greater Toronto. As a matter of fact, I have been in most of them. Anyone visiting those offices at almost any time during the past months would realize how overcrowded they are and how inadequate is the accommodation in which those who administer this act are obliged to work. I had hoped that the minister would give consideration particularly to those who are the managers of those offices. I pointed out here previously the nature of the responsibility which these men assume and the qualifications which are required in those who are to manage efficiently some of these larger employment service offices.

These persons certainly warrant a much higher category of wages or salaries than those they are receiving at the present time.
Those are some of the shortcomings of the present amendments, as I see them, and the extent to which these amendments fail to measure up to the advance publicity which this act has received or to meet the present-day pressing needs. I know that in itself unemployment insurance cannot be expected to care for all those who may become unemployed and to do so indefinitely; certainly that is so if that fund is to remain actuarially sound. I suppose any unemployment insurance fund which was to provide for all the unemployed for indefinite periods of unemployment would have to be one that would make subsidies from the federal treasury from time to time a part of the fund. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre quoted the Minister of National Health and Welfare, when he was speaking at the time of the inauguration of the fund in 1940, as follows, as reported at page 2673 of Hansard:
.	.	. unemployment Insurance in itself is not
sufficient to meet the needs presented by a situation of that sort and must be related to the question of unemployment relief, . . .
As a matter of fact, the maintenance of employment and protection against unemployment are both parts of the same problem. The present unemployment insurance is only a partial protection against unemployment. This revision of the act fails to meet that over-all problem. The over-all problem consists of both the maintenance of employment and protection against unemployment.
I realize that the federal government at the present time takes the position that the maintenance of employment or the maintenance of conditions favourable to employment is a federal responsibility and that the maintenance of the unemployment insurance fund is a federal responsibility but that it maintains that the residual problem, namely the protection of the employable unemployed who are without unemployment insurance benefits, is a provincial responsibility until such time as the provinces are unable to meet that responsibility. That appears to be the official position taken by the federal parliament at the present time.
For the life of me I fail to see by what logic or on what grounds the government has reached that conclusion. I fail to see how the government can possibly reach the conclusion that the most serious part of protection against unemployment must be left on the doorstep of the provincial government or the municipality. As a matter of fact, most of the inquiries which have been made into this
Unemployment Insurance Act problem-including the inquiry by the unemployment insurance commission, by the Sirois commission and by the government itself in 1945-all agree that this is a federal responsibility. The government itself in 1945 was agreed that not only were the maintenance of employment and the maintenance of the unemployment insurance fund federal responsibilities but that protection against unemployment was a federal responsibility.
When one considers the nature of that problem, one fails to see how any organization to deal with it can possibly be successfully administered by a provincial or a municipal government. If those who move from place to place in search of work are not to be penalized for so doing, we must have some uniform national system of unemployment protection. Otherwise those who move from one province to another or from one municipality to another are going to be penalized. If unemployed Canadians are to be treated in all the provinces by the same standards and are to receive the same treatment, this whole problem of protection against unemployment must be administered by some such organization as the unemployment insurance offices or some organization under federal direction which will give some uniformity of treatment to unemployed people, regardless of the province or the municipality in which they are. Certainly, whether or not the federal government admits it, the country today believes that responsibility for protection against unemployment is a federal matter, and we think that the major share of that responsibility, both in connection with financing and organizing for its administration, rests with the federal government. These facts were recognized by the government in 1940. I have before me a brief presented to the members of parliament from the Toronto district on Saturday morning by the Toronto branch of the Canadian association of social workers.

For many months now we have had officials working on the problem of insurance coverage for them in the most serious and intensive fashion. I have not given up hope that we may find a solution. I know it will not be a perfect solution but I hope we can find a good solution somewhere, whether it comes within the field of unemployment insurance, under some special measure administered by the Department of Fisheries, or a combination of both.
But what I can say, as far as this measure is concerned, is that if, as and when a solution is found with respect to unemployment insurance, it will be possible for fishermen so recommended for inclusion to be brought within the legislation without any further amendment of the act. The hon. member for Hamilton West says that the coverage should be as wide as possible. That unquestionably continues to be the policy of the government, and that is why I did not mention it yesterday. Now, it is not as easy as it looks, and I am sure that hon. members realize that. I am going to take only one example. We live and work in a free economy and believe that our various organizations have a right to express themselves without our pushing them around and imposing something upon them. In the very mild and friendly discussion on the resolution that took place yesterday one hon. member said something to the effect that rumours had been heard that the Minister of Labour was going to bring hospital workers under unemployment insurance, and why in the world was the minister delaying so long?
I did not see that report in the press but it must have been somewhere because on my desk this morning I had wires from the chairmen of hospital boards saying in effect, "For heaven's sake, don't do it". I mention

that as an example. You will recall that the former minister of finance introduced last year quite a mild little measure affecting the welfare of our federal civil servants on the assumption that it would apply 100 per cent to everybody. You will recall what happened under the banner of freedom with respect to that measure. What happened under the banner of freedom as to that measure would be small business compared with what would happen under the banner of freedom if the Minister of Labour were to say, without a good deal of prior spade work, if you like, that 100 per cent of federal civil servants were going to be brought under this legislation on this day in April, 1955. But I will say that we are from month to month bringing in any groups that can be brought in and we can always do it; we do not have to amend the act. Quite a number of members mentioned that point.
The point concerning supplementary benefits and their effect upon the period this year, I shall leave until the end of my remarks. I shall make a short reference now to two points that were mentioned by many, one of them concerning the women. This point is always forcibly put forward by the hon. member for Cape Breton South as well as the hon. member for Hamilton West. I will undertake now to have still another look at that regulation. It is a regulation, and I am confident it is one that has to be there in some form. It is not there because of discrimination, but simply because a woman is a different sort of individual from a man, with all the implications that go with that. It is the desire of the government, and the desire of the commission, that that regulation should only affect the few who might be tempted to take advantage of the situation to the detriment of the thousands of others who are paying into the insurance fund. But we will have another look at it this winter.
The other point mentioned by many members concerned the interesting item of the guaranteed annual wage, on which I shall only make two comments. One of them is that during the last five years I have been Minister of Labour I have learned one thing, and that is that while an item is in the process of discussion under collective bargaining, the federal government or Department of Labour should not interject itself. At the same time, I add quickly that the federal Department of Labour should not keep its eyes and ears closed but its officials, as they are doing, should keep the situation under review and know what is happening so they will at least be able to think intelligently about it. I shall touch upon the 50433-172i
Unemployment Insurance Act other points mentioned by the hon. member for Hamilton West as I come to them.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre rather poked fun at me by saying that I was like Gaul. I was very much interested in following him as he traced areas of my own research in his historical review. I found it, as a matter of fact, a very interesting survey with which I take no exception at all. However, he did leave me rather up in the air in the speech I made to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association last summer. The facts of that are simply these. On invitation, I went out to Jasper and, after a good deal of sweat and walking in the mountains because of the flood, I talked to the association on seasonal unemployment. I did state that there were certain fixed charges, certain fixed things they would have anyhow and the moral of the speech was to the effect, why not use these fixed facilities that you have to have to make sure your employees work a full year rather than being seasonally unemployed in the wintertime. That was the essence of the message. It was not related to the guaranteed annual wage, but I will admit it was related to the same objective, namely, providing year-round work during the winter months.
I can say this this afternoon, that the experiments we have been carrying out in this regard are not going to be the entire cure of unemployment. However, long before next winter we shall learn how big a dent, if it can make a dent, this program can make in seasonal unemployment. If it is a reasonably sized dent, then what we can do federally we are going to do in co-operation with all the other forces. I do not know yet how far we can go, but in the experiments we have conducted this winter the great labour organizations and organized industry have co-operated in the fullest possible fashion.
The leader of the Social Credit party expressed his general approval of this measure, as did the representatives of that party who spoke when the resolution was introduced in 1940. I thank him for his kind words. I also wish to thank the hon. member for Welland for expressing his opinion that, by and large, what he sees coming forward in this legislation fulfils what he had in mind when he placed his resolution on the order paper some time last November.
Now, the hon. member for Broadview spoke, and I was glad to give him an opportunity to tell his Texas story concerning the grasshopper. In my opinion he took an extraordinary stand when he gave us the impression he was prepared to place no limit upon the extension of these benefits. I can tell you today, Mr. Chairman, that not only management but the national labour organizations of

Unemployment Insurance Act this country would look with the utmost concern upon an unlimited extension of these benefits. They, as well as the government, are anxious that this plan shall be on a sound financial basis, and it is easy to see the reason for that. During these 14 years, both of these groups have been making their contributions to this fund day after day and week after week. They have been making these contributions on the understanding that the fund is to be maintained financially sound. The government and any minister of labour must, therefore, to a degree, look upon this as a trust fund on behalf of the two parties concerned, as well as on behalf of the taxpayer. If any minister of labour, without going back and reviewing the whole ground once more, were to say that benefits may be given to a few people for an unlimited period from the money contributed by a great many who want to be sure when they become unemployed that assistance will be there, it would in my opinion be a violation of that trust.

Yes, but without mentioning
any limit.
The hon. member for Nanaimo also discussed the guaranteed annual wage. I believe I have covered the points put forward by all hon. members except those by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
Among other things he said that the heads of our great industries were not using our national employment service. With all due respect I say that is not entirely true. However, it is true to say that many of them do maintain their own employment offices or, if you like, their own aptitude assessment offices. Great companies like General Motors at Oshawa, for one, do use our services in a big way; but since such companies, in this modem age, have so many technical jobs to carry out they quite naturally depend upon their own people to assess the qualifications for those jobs. This they can do more specifically than can our

staff. I should like to go that far in correcting the record to show that a great many of our large industrial organizations do use the national employment service.
The hon. member said that unemployment insurance is no good to those who have exhausted their benefits 100 per cent. A good many other hon. members said the same thing. My hon. friend quoted two industries which have been very much to the fore in unemployment and very much in the minds of many of us, namely the soft coal industry and the textile industry. If ever there were examples of personnel exhausting their benefits 100 per cent they were in the two communities he mentioned, one at Westville, the soft coal industry, and one at Marysville, a cotton textile industry. I happen to have a very intimate knowledge of both, since both are near my home.
This afternoon I am going to say a word about Westville. A little over a year ago, on the recommendation of my colleagues the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and the cabinet minister representing Nova Scotia, the Minister of Public Works, and at the needling of the hon. member for Pictou, we recommended to our colleagues in the government that we take a step, in co-operation with the province of Nova Scotia, that was completely uneconomical, namely that certain subsidies should be continued for another six months if the province of Nova Scotia did certain things and if the management of the industry did certain things, with the definite and specific object of extending for another six months the life of the project in Westville to make employment possible for those who had been thrown out of work before they reached 100 per cent of their insurance benefits.
From time to time since then I have informed the three gentlemen I have mentioned of the progress made. Without going into details, it is the kind of thing you cannot transfer to Windsor, to Montreal, or to Sault Ste. Marie, but in pleasant, snug little places like Westville and Marysville, you can do something because it is much easier to encompass the situation. In co-operation with the provinces concerned, under schedule M of our Vocational Training Co-ordination Act which, as hon. members know, contains a provision for training at the same time one is receiving benefits, a great deal has been done in both places. In fact, in these places I am looking forward to the time within a very few months when the situation may be liquidated with the least possible hardship and the fewest possible number of people left unemployed, or older people left without some more appropriate means for their care.

I am referring not only to old age pensions for those over 70 and other pensions for those between 65 and 70 and not only to the rehabilitation program. The sort of thing I am referring to has to do with the older person who has lost his employment, who has used up his regular benefits and his supplementary benefits, and for whom a job cannot be found. Even though we are trying hard, and with some success, to find jobs for older workers, some other means must be provided. I agree with that entirely. Some other, as I said yesterday, more appropriate means should be provided.
So far as Westville is concerned, I have mentioned one of those means. Another which is not so clear is what is going to happen to those who never took advantage of the labour benefits and for whom there is no provision at all. Well, Mr. Chairman, that was recognized here. For those long-term unemployed it was recognized and that is the reason we provided for a three-year period of grace, in the hope that the gap might be filled before the three years were up. As far as I am concerned, if perchance I am minister of labour three years hence, I shall certainly want to look at the picture again, if no more appropriate means is provided for them than there is at the present time, though I think there will be.
The hon. member for Kootenay West agreed with my expression of policy but with respect to part 3, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre called it, he did not agree with the way in which it was put into effect. The main reason he did not agree with that was, if I followed him closely, on account of the point I have just been discussing. He said we were making a retreat because we were cutting down the long-term benefit period of the old act. I claim we are not making a retreat, because for the three years we are seeing to it that the people who are now insured shall receive just as good or better benefits in those three years as they would have received if the act had not been changed.
With respect to the point made by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, having to do with the appeal under the act, that he would like to see the matter settled on the decision of the local referees rather than having it finally go for appeal to the umpire, I was glad to hear his comments on the fairness and capacity of the local board of referees. The only reason the machinery set up a central umpire was to give, as in the veterans legislation and other legislation, the applicant one more opportunity to win his case by taking it to yet another appeal in the
Unemployment Insurance Act hope of getting more consideration. However, I shall be glad to have the point of view that he expressed presented to the committee when it meets.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that I have left a number of points unanswered, but I shall be glad to search Hansard during the Easter recess and try to rectify any omissions. But there is one point I have put off to the end, and that has to do with the extent of supplementary or seasonal benefits this year. From now on I shall call them seasonal benefits so as not to get it mixed.
Practically every hon. member who spoke referred to his concern about this winter. I can tell the committee that the government has also felt concern about this. I can remember that last year at this time many insured workers were on seasonal or supplementary benefits and were looking forward to April 15, realizing, as somebody put it, that there would be no more for them, that that would be the end. They were wondering what was going to happen.
I kept in close touch with things and to my surprise it worked out reasonably well. In other words the change-over was gradual, and apparently there was no serious hardship. I did not consider only what came to my attention; to some extent I went out to see if it was true. That was last year.
In the discussion yesterday some suggested that the supplementary period should start in December. Then I think someone suggested that the governor in council should be allowed to decide when it would end, based on the weather in any part of Canada. Others suggested that it should be extended beyond April 15 for longer or shorter periods.
I shall deal first with the suggestion that it start before the first of the year. I am sure that would be useful, but our experience has shown that the impact of summer and fall earnings carry over the Christmas holidays into a time after January 1, when for all unemployed some added resources are most useful. Therefore we believe that the first of the year is most appropriate as a starting point.
At this juncture I should like also to say that I am confident the dates of start and finish must be the same all across Canada. As Minister of Labour I would hate to be put into the position of having to recommend to the governor in council when each seasonal benefit period should end. I am sure there would be a great contest as to whether the storm which I believe happened the day before yesterday in Alberta was worse than the spring flood which probably will be coming along in a few weeks on the Grand river

Unemployment Insurance Act and the effect of each on spring employment. It would be an impossible position for the government to have to decide those things each spring, based on the weather or the length of the winter.

speechtext: It is a fair weather government.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Quite true. Having set the time, I think you must be fairly rigid. We were rigid at the beginning. We set the period as January 1 to April 1. Then we went on with the one-cent business which worked out a lot better than we thought it would. Then we cautiously put on another couple of weeks to the seasonal benefit period and said we would make it go to the middle of April. But it is obvious from what I presented yesterday, that under the new arrangement and by mopping up that one cent and in the general revision proposed, we feel that we can do something much more useful now.
Back in 1950 the supplementary benefits were tailored especially for Canada, for our heavy winter and the unemployment resulting therefrom. It was felt that we should deliberately place the weight of our benefits on the winter months. If the over-all structure of the act was sound in 1950, then it was realized that any benefits we concentrated on the winter season would have to be taken away from the year-round benefits if this one cent did not make up the difference.
It is important to remember also that a great number of the insured workers are in employment which rides along through the year with winter, spring and summer, making very little difference in the amount of unemployment in those industries. We had to be careful as to what was happening during the winter. Back in 1950 an estimate was made of the concentration of full resources which would be aimed at the winter. That might be called X. It was then a question as to how that quantity X could be handled most usefully and equitably during any winter. After our first extension it became evident that this X was a much more buoyant amount than perhaps was anticipated.
A few weeks ago I took some of these suggestions home with me, and on looking through them I was greatly pleased with what appeared to me to be a surprising effect upon this winter and future winters. After all if our X is a good-sized amount and it is broken down into various shares for the purpose of a worker getting through a difficult winter, it does not matter whether that amount is spread over three or four months, or whether it comes in two or three months, or in 15, 20 or 25 weeks.

Here is the point I think we overlooked when we rushed through the supplementary benefits in January. Let us take a worker who this year and last year accumulated- we do not need to go into the background -exactly the same seasonal benefits each year. Take the worker who is in receipt of regular benefits of $24 per week. Last year the seasonal benefits were roughly 70 per cent of $24, which amounts to $17. Last year the minimum number of weeks a worker could have in the seasonal period was six. I will ask the hon. member for Hamilton West to check me on this, but I believe that six multiplied by $17 gives a total of $102. That is the amount of X that that man could have last year, and it did not matter how it was spread out. This year that same man can get seasonal benefits for 10 weeks at $24 a week, which gives a total of $240.
I think this provides a good answer to the demand to extend the period. We have nearly trebled the amount of money paid in the same period, and after all that is what counts. In case anyone thinks I am giving a distorted picture by taking the top man, let us consider the man in the lowest category and see what he will get this winter. Last winter under our old plan the lowest paid married man could get 70 per cent of $4.80 per week; that was all. Last year during the seasonal benefit period he could get 3 weeks, multiplied by $3.60, which is 70 per cent, or $10.80.
This year he can get 10 weeks multiplied by $4.80 or $48, which in this case is five times better than it was last year.
I wanted to mention these things because we do not intend to extend the seasonal benefit period this year. As a matter of fact we could not extend the period unless we rushed this bill through and made it law by tomorrow. As the 15th of the month comes during the Easter recess I felt the house should have that much reassurance on behalf of those who formally come to the end of their benefit period on the 15th of April but in reality, due to the working of the machine the receipt of the last cheques will be spread over the last half of April and in some cases extend into May. I join with hon. members in expressing the hope that we might move into the spring period without any serious hardship in that regard.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Die-fenbaker for the second reading of Bill No. 186, to amend the Criminal Code (nuisance).

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO WATER POLLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) is not in his seat this afternoon because I want to make a few comments with regard to what he said on March 18.
In the debate we had last year the minister made what I thought was a good move when he suggested that an interprovincial water board be given power to control interprovincial rivers, or to control the pollution in interprovincial rivers. The meeting was called, as was suggested, and the other day the minister gave a report of what took place at that meeting. The result was that the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba and the dominion government agreed to the setting up of this board, but the province of Alberta did not agree.
The minister, however, went on to give a report of what this meeting had done and the recommendations it had made. He said that the province of Alberta was controlling the situation at the present time. That is correct; that is the situation at the present time. But the people whom I represent are still worried. They wonder what would happen if at some time in the future the Alberta government should get a little bit careless, perhaps, and not look after this situation in the way it should. What have they to protect them from a recurrence of pollution? What protection have they? They simply have nothing, as far as I can see.
I want to support this amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert because, in spite of what the minister said, I think it clarifies section 165 of the Criminal Code. I think it makes it clearer to anybody-especially to a person like myself, an

Criminal Code
ordinary layman-that it is a crime to pollute the water of any interprovincial river. In speaking on March 18 the minister, as reported at page 2174 of Hansard, had this to say:
Having regard to the fact that in the Alberta provincial law and in the federal Fisheries Act there are provisions that prohibit the discharge of effluents and the placing of waste in the Saskatchewan river in Alberta-
I want to say something about the Fisheries Act because last year on February 5, I asked the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) this question, as reported at page 1812 of Hansard:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. Will the minister have an inspection made of the fish life in the North Saskatchewan river to determine whether the pollution of the water in that river is killing or affecting the health of the fish in that river?
This is what the Minister of Fisheries said in answer to that question:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of this question. There is no question that under the British North America Act legislative jurisdiction over fisheries rests with the federal government. However, by agreement with the government of Canada in 1930 the three prairie provinces took over the responsibility of administering their own natural resources, including fisheries. Since that date provincial officers enforce federal fisheries conservation laws. The federal government does not maintain any staff in those provinces for this purpose. Therefore the inspection of the alleged pollution of the North Saskatchewan river would primarily be the responsibility of the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
There is no question whatsoever about the fact that the Fisheries Act which is enforced in those provinces by the provincial authorities contains sufficient authority.
I agree with that statement. But I would point out that if one province causes pollution affecting another province, the province affected has no protection. It does not matter which province it is that does it. It might be the province of Saskatchewan next time which would cause pollution and harm the province of Manitoba. Under this act the province of Manitoba has absolutely no protection whatsoever. I continue with the quotation from the minister's answer:
Perhaps if I just read subsection 2 of section 33 of the Fisheries Act, it will be seen how wide the powers are. Subsection 2 of section 33 reads as follows:
"No person shall cause or knowingly permit to pass into, or put or knowingly permit to be put, lime, chemical substances or drugs, poisonous matter, dead or decaying fish, or remains thereof, mill rubbish or sawdust or any other deleterious substance or thing, whether the same is of a like character to the substances named in this section or not, in any water frequented by fish, or that flows into such water, nor on ice over either such waters."

I want to point out that the wording of the amendment is quite similar to that of the Fisheries Act. The amendment reads as follows:
Every owner, lessee, or person operating any industrial plant, oil refinery, chemical works, sawmill or other plant or works, or any other person, who discharges or throws or allows to be discharged or thrown any noxious waste product, raw sewage, oil, sawdust, chemical or other matter or thing into a river, stream or other water any part of which is interprovincial or which flows into any interprovincial water, which has the effect of endangering the lives, safety, health or comfort of the public is guilty of
(a)	an indictable offence and is liable to a fine of ten thousand dollars for a first offence and of twenty thousand dollars for a second offence, or
(b)	an offence punishable on summary conviction.
As I said before, this amendment is quite similar to the Fisheries Act. It is quite evident that the Department of Fisheries considered that it was necessary to have in the act something which would prevent the putting in the rivers of anything that would harm the fish. It seems to me that if we are interested in the welfare of fish we should certainly be equally interested in the welfare and health of our people.
This question is not dead. It is still quite a live question in my province. Only a few days ago-on March 31, to be exact-in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, which is a paper that usually supports the government, there appeared an editorial which is headed "Unsound Case" and which reads as follows:
Who is there that does not agree with Mr. Garson that the best way to deal with pollution in interprovincial rivers is through co-operation of health authorities in the various provinces? But can Mr. Garson suggest what is to be done if one of the provinces refuses to co-operate?
At this point I want to interject that I am not accusing the Alberta government at this time of not co-operating. They are not co-operating as part of an interprovincial board, but I believe they are making a pretty good job of controlling pollution at the present time. The editorial continues:
That is the situation now with regard to the North Saskatchewan river which was polluted a year ago, to the great inconvenience of residents living along it. Manitoba and Saskatchewan are agreed on a joint commission which would have advisory jurisdiction over interprovincial waters in the western provinces. Alberta so far has not agreed to co-operate fully, although that province has pledged to control pollution within its borders by unilateral action.
Such a pledge is better than no agreement at all; but it is not as good as a broader arrangement which would cover every situation, as a federal law would do. Mr. Garson has always countered this argument by noting that any law prohibiting pollution of interprovincial waters anywhere in Canada would complicate the situation in eastern Canada. We gather by implication that he is saying that many interprovincial rivers in eastern Canada are now being polluted, and that to forbid

this would harass both Industries and municipalities. II this is his point, then on this matter he is basing his argument on convenience rather than principle. Perhaps it does appear expedient to allow pollution of eastern waters to continue, but it is not wise in principle, as the future may demonstrate. The federal government would be on sounder ground if it faced up to this matter now, and undertook to control interprovincial waters with regard to pollution.
I do not believe the bill before us is a solution to the problem of pollution. Pollution has to be stopped before it starts if effective control is to be exercised. However, I believe the amendment might be a better deterrent than subsection 2 of section 165 of the Criminal Code. Perhaps, as the minister said, the penalty is too light; but I was sold on the suggestion made by the minister last year, as I have said before, that an interprovincial water board be given powers to prevent pollution. I think such a board could set up a licensing system that could control effectively what effluents and the amounts thereof could be discharged into an interprovincial river, and where pollution did take place such licences could be cancelled.
It is the feeling now of the provincial government and the people of the constituency I represent that the federal government should accept the responsibility of preventive control. This view is also held by many other people. Now that the Alberta government has refused to become a party to an interprovincial water board assuming control, where are we if that government falls down on the job? We in the province of Saskatchewan have to depend on the good offices of the Alberta government, and the people of Battle-ford are living in dread of a recurrence of last winter's pollution.
The Alberta government, while disagreeing with the idea of such a board, have stated that they will look after the problem themselves, and it would appear that they are doing so. But the people of Battleford remember the statement made to the delegation last spring by Dr. Somerville. I was a member of the delegation that went to the city of Edmonton. We interviewed Dr. Cross and Dr. Somerville and one of his engineers, and we also went to the plant. But one statement made by Dr. Somerville stood out and caused us considerable worry, and is still doing so. He said that the province of Alberta is being industrialized very rapidly. He said that industries are coming in at a tremendous rate, and it is going to be almost impossible to prevent pollution. He went on to suggest that the city of Prince Albert, the town of Battleford and the mental institution in North Battleford try to find a new source of water supply.
Canada Elections Act
We were pretty much flabbergasted when Dr. Somerville made that statement, and that is the reason I am on my feet today. That is also the reason the people of my constituency are still worried. If industries continue to come into Alberta, and if an industry happens to be a borderline case-perhaps it will pollute the river and perhaps it will not- it may be that the Alberta government which, as I have already said, is doing a good job now, might be persuaded to take a chance and let that industry discharge effluents into the river, thus bringing about another period of pollution. I want to warn both the Alberta government and the federal government that the people along the North Saskatchewan river will not tolerate further pollution, and if it does take place strong pressure is going to be put on the federal government to take action. The federal government has now created a precedent bytaking control under recent legislation of that portion of international rivers which lies within Canada. They can hardly refuse to accept the responsibility of looking after the pollution of interprovincial rivers and the health of the people of all the provinces concerned, especially the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, if the province of Alberta falls down on the job and does not see to it that pollution does not take place again.

I think that angle of the matter was dealt with very well by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
However, I did point out that after we are elected to the House of Commons and come

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to present a grievance to this house on the motion to go into supply, I should like to say first that in general law enforcement is not the direct concern of this house; it is primarily the concern of the provincial and municipal authorities. However when the action, or rather the inaction, 50433-1734
Law Enforcement
of a federal department results in a set of conditions under which certain illegal activities are carried out by those who do not appear to be Canadian citizens, the time has arrived for the situation to be brought to the attention of the house so that some action may be taken.
Since my grievance concerns the continued presence in Canada of non-Canadians of questionable character it is obviously the responsibility of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. This department must accept the responsibility for not having dealt with United States gamblers and big-time bookies who have operated in Canada for the past two years without interference save by municipal authorities. Before I have finished this presentation I shall name names and cite cases to document this charge.
The basis of the invasion of Canada by these United States racketeers goes back to the Kefauver investigation in the United States. Following that investigation United States syndicates which had been there disclosed began to move into Canada and located themselves in Montreal in 1952, because the United States government had passed a law requiring all bookmakers to register, pay a fee of $50 and keep elaborate written records of all their transactions. Severe fines and penalties were provided for those who disobeyed these regulations.
Since it is obvious that operations of this kind do not flourish under any kind of regulation or restraint, and these conditions were making it most difficult for them to operate, the bookmakers in search of a more favourable climate turned to Canada. They could locate where they wished, because as far as convenience in carrying on their business is concerned it might be noted that the practice of bookmaking requires little more than a telephone and an office. A bookmaker operates on a split second schedule. In the United States his principal method of communication is the leased wire service, but here in Canada he depends upon the long distance telephone. In one case to which I shall refer subsequently it is stated that the long distance telephone bills of one organization which was uncovered amounted to something over $6,000 a month.
Since I am here making reference to telephone service in Canada I should point out in all fairness that it is almost impossible for the Bell Telephone Company to stop the illegal use of its lines and equipment unless that is reported upon by the police authorities. They are legally obliged to give these services wherever possible and whenever anyone requests them. In applying for the service the applicant must state that he proposes to

Law Enforcement
use it for legal purposes. On February 22, 1955, I asked the following question of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Picker sgill):
Since Montreal police have confirmed that a large number of notorious American thugs have entered Canada illegally and are currently resident in and around Montreal, is there no process by which the Department of Citizenship and Immigration can locate and deal with such undesirables?
The minister replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, just before I came into the house I received a notice from the hon. gentleman that he was going to ask the question he has just put in the house. I anticipated a question of this nature. Like the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace, I had advice of the report in the Montreal Star. I made immediate inquiries of the appropriate officials of the department.
Then later:
I am advised that somewhat similar reports were brought to the attention of the R.C.M.P. and the immigration branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and that an investigation has been under way for some time to see whether there has been any violation of the laws which the federal government has the responsibility of enforcing:	and that, of course, includes the
Immigration Act.
I do not think there is anything useful I can add to this answer until this investigation has been completed.
That was over five weeks ago. The fact that the minister could give an answer such as that at that point indicates almost unbelievable inefficiency in the way he operates his department. In the first place the men to whom I referred had at that time been in Canada for approximately two years, during the greater portion of which their presence in this country had been to say the least rumoured and discussed. Yet the minister made no inquiries whatsoever about them until I raised the point in this house; at least that was the purport of his answer.
The basic point at issue is whether or not the minister and his officials should have been aware of this illegal activity some considerable time before I raised the matter in the house. I submit that they certainly should. Besides having been a matter of discussion around Montreal for some two years the whole situation had been a matter of public record in Montreal for almost two months before the minister, prodded by my questioning, even said he would look into it. I should like now to present him with a little evidence in support of this complaint.
A raid by the Montreal police on January 1, 1955, at 1421 Bleury street revealed the existence of a gambling establishment with nine telephones, along with telephone bills, betting slips, racing publications and typewriters. This is the establishment to which

I referred earlier with telephone bills averaging $6,000 a month. In its issue of January 5, 1955, the Montreal Herald, in addition to giving the previous information, had this to
say:
Details of the operation have remained secret although the identity of many of the American gamblers handling the business is commonly known. The move to Montreal came largely as part of an attempt to avoid the attention of American federal law enforcement agencies where interstate transactions were involved.
The same story dealt at some length with a raid on Tuesday, January 4, 1955, on the offices of an organization called the Seaway Construction Company, located on Stanley street in Montreal. A Mr. Camille Joseph was arrested in this raid, and the story contains this interesting statement referring to Mr. Joseph:
Detectives said he claimed to come from San Antonio, Texas.
I have had somebody look further into this case and am informed that certain claims were made that this man is an American and certain claims were made that he is a Canadian. However, these reports identify him as an American. The January 6, 1955, issue of the Montreal Herald contains an article indicating that local gambling activities have been partly discontinued, but there is the following paragraph regarding those which have continued:
Main gambling activities here lately have been the American lay-off operations-underwriting the bets of American bookies by long distance telephone-and the chartered gambling clubs, legal as long as they observe certain rules.
We now see that some two months before my question in this house it became a matter of public record in Montreal that there had been American infiltration into this illegal field. Yet at the time of my asking my question it was obvious that the minister knew nothing about the situation, even though his department had been conducting an investigation for some time-and I quote from the minister's reply-
-to see whether there had been any violation of the laws which the federal government has the responsibility of enforcing; and that, of course, includes the Immigration Act.
I suggest that this is one case to start with, where if the minister and his officials were on their toes they would have dealt with the offender properly and been in a position to report to this house when the question was raised.
Let us now turn to the situation as it existed on February 22, when the question was raised in the house. Through a newspaper story which appeared in the Toronto Telegram of that date I propose to show that

more than adequate information was available to permit the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to deal adequately with the situation either on or before that date. I use the newspaper story, first because it is a matter of public record and second because if a working newspaperman could procure the information contained in this story it could surely have been procured by the government through the extensive facilities and resources of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The story is headlined, "United States Gang Set Up Headquarters in Quebec" and it carries the byline of Jack Macbeth.
As I said, I propose to put this story on the record not so much to bolster my facts as to show in the first place the information which was available to the department, and second to show what an ordinary newspaperman-a working newspaperman, because no newspapermen are ordinary-could find out through his own efforts. The story reads-
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, as this story was denied, I believe, by the chief of police in Montreal in the newspapers the following day, I wonder-
How do you know; you have not heard the story?
According to the newspaper reports the following day it was denied, and I am wondering if this is not a little irrelevant.
You have not heard it yet.
I read it.
You are anticipating it.

The
interjection of the minister, Mr. Speaker, will be dealt with in due course. I think he would be well advised to read the Montreal newspapers much more carefully both before and after any event.
